A sedentary control group (CON) with low habitual physical activity was also recruited. In total, 80 college students participated. Physical activity (PA) was assessed using a standardized questionnaire. All participants underwent structural MRI and resting-state fMRI to derive gray matter volume (GMV), fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), degree centrality (DC), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and functional connectivity (FC) within parietal subregions (S1, SPL, AG, and SMG). Supplementary SPL-based FC analyses further examined connectivity with regions of the broader visuospatial and sensorimotor network. Visual tracking was assessed using a multiple object tracking (MOT) task across three difficulty levels. RESULTS: PA levels were significantly higher in all athlete groups than in sedentary controls, with no differences among athlete groups. Across structural and resting-state functional measures, the most consistent group differences were selectively concentrated in S1 and SPL, whereas effects involving other parietal regions were less consistent across measures. Specifically, the ESU group exhibited the highest bilateral S1 GMV, the SCP group showed the highest bilateral SPL GMV, and the IPS group demonstrated the highest fALFF in both S1 and SPL. The IPS group also showed the highest ReHo in bilateral SPL. FC differed significantly across several parietal connections, with distinct connectivity patterns across the three athlete groups. MOT accuracy differed significantly across groups at all difficulty levels, with the ESU and IPS groups outperforming the SCP and CON groups overall. Across all participants, multiple S1 and SPL metrics showed modest associations with MOT performance (r = 0.20-0.40). Within athlete subgroups, stronger and task-specific associations were observed, particularly in the SCP and IPS groups (r = 0.50-0.80). CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify distinct structural and functional patterns predominantly involving S1 and SPL across different motor participation profiles, despite comparable overall physical activity levels among the athlete groups. Such parietal differences are accompanied by difficulty-dependent differences in visual tracking performance and heterogeneous brain-behavior associations. Together, the results highlight S1 and SPL as the parietal regions showing the most consistent differentiation across structural and functional measures in association with distinct motor participation profiles and visual tracking performance, and provide a focused empirical basis for future investigations into the sources of this heterogeneity.

articles.title: A shape deformation-based framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks.
articles.abstract: Individualized morphological brain networks have emerged as an important framework for imaging-based connectomics. However, existing methods have focused predominantly on the cerebral cortex, leaving subcortical structures largely unexplored despite their central roles in cognition and neuropsychiatric disorders. Here, we developed a novel framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks from structural magnetic resonance imaging. Specifically, subcortical surfaces were reconstructed using a Point2Mesh-optimized multilayer perceptron architecture and vertex-wise shape deformation was quantified as the signed Euclidean distance between each vertex on an individual mesh and the corresponding vertex on the group-average template mesh. Interregional morphological connectivity in local shape deformation distributions was subsequently estimated using Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Applying this approach to the Human Connectome Project dataset, we found that subcortical morphological networks exhibited complex topological organization, including small-world architecture, modular organization, and highly connected hubs, which were consistently preserved at finer subregional scales. Analyses using an independent test-retest dataset further demonstrated fair-to-good reliability of these network properties. Importantly, these shape deformation-based networks showed significant coupling with subcortical functional networks estimated from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Leveraging large-scale multisite clinical datasets, we further demonstrated alterations of subcortical morphological networks in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. Schizophrenia was characterized predominantly by right caudate-centered disruptions in morphological connectivity and nodal centrality, whereas major depressive disorder exhibited alterations only in nodal centrality of the right amygdala. Together, these findings establish a novel and reliable framework for investigating subcortical morphological network organization in the human brain across both healthy and psychiatric populations.

articles.title: Study on the capture and thrombolytic efficacy of magnetic particle clusters under a deeply focused rotating magnetic field.
articles.abstract: Magnetic particle-mediated targeted delivery of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), assisted by a rotating magnetic field (RMF), represents a highly promising approach for the treatment of venous thrombosis. However, existing magnetic strategies face bottlenecks in deep tissues and complex hemodynamics due to poor focusing and weak flow resistance. Consequently, flow washout induces particle escape, while magnetic attenuation severely limits the clusters ' operating range and fluid perturbation. Achieving deep focusing and flow-resistant retention of magnetic particle clusters (MPCs) under deep-tissue, high-flow conditions remains a critical challenge for the clinical translation of this technology. To this end, a novel deeply focused rotating magnetic field (DF-RMF) system driven by dual synchronized rotating permanent magnets is developed. It establishes an axial magnetic focusing zone with dual-peak confinement and continuous centripetal properties to effectively counteract fluid drag. Simulations and in vitro flow experiments demonstrate that the DF-RMF stably confines magnetic particle clusters as compact, continuously rotating clusters at the lumen center. This effectively expands their geometric working boundaries and significantly enhances synergistic thrombolytic efficacy. Even at distances up to 5 cm or under the normal physiological flow velocity of lower extremity veins (~14 cm/s), the system maintains a substantial particle retention rate. Rotating synchronously under the DF-RMF, the clusters generate mechanical shear while inducing intense microfluidic circulation and pressure fluctuations. This physically disrupts the thrombus and accelerates interfacial tPA transport to boost fibrinolysis, achieving complete in vitro recanalization with a removal rate ~5 times that of tPA alone. This study provides a novel physical modulation strategy with translational potential for deep, precision targeted delivery and synergistic mechanical-biochemical thrombolysis in complex blood flow environments.

articles.title: Imaging-derived coronary fractional flow reserve: advances in physics-based, machine learning, and physics-informed methods.
articles.abstract: Purpose of Review Imaging-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR) is rapidly evolving beyond conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based pipelines toward machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and physics-informed approaches that enable fast, wire-free, and scalable functional assessment of coronary artery stenosis. This review synthesizes recent advances in computed tomography (CT)-and angiography-based FFR measurement, with particular emphasis on emerging physics-informed neural networks and neural operators (PINNs and PINOs), as well as key considerations for their clinical translation.Recent Findings ML/DL approaches have markedly improved automation and computational speed, enabling prediction of pressure and FFR from anatomical descriptors or angiographic contrast dynamics. However, their real-world performance and generalizability can remain variable and sensitive to domain shift, due to multi-center heterogeneity, interpretability challenges, and differences in acquisition protocols and image quality. Physics-informed learning introduces conservation structure and boundary-condition consistency into model training, improving generalizability and reducing dependence on dense supervision while maintaining rapid inference. Recent evaluation trends increasingly highlight deployment-oriented metrics, including calibration, uncertainty quantification, and quality-control gatekeeping, as essential for safe clinical use.SummaryThe field is converging toward imaging-derived FFR methods that are faster, more automated, and more reliable. While ML/DL offers substantial efficiency gains, physics-informed frameworks such as PINNs and PINOs may provide a more robust balance between speed and physical consistency. Prospective multi-center validation and standardized evaluation will be critical to support broad and safe clinical adoption.

articles.title: Dimensionality reduction for partial-volume correction in quantitative SPECT.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this paper is to develop a method for region-based post-reconstruction partial-volume correction (PVC) of SPECT images, which explicitly estimates the mean activity concentration in regions without assuming strict intra-regional uniformity. APPROACH: Partial-volume correction was applied to177Lu-SPECT images obtained from the simulation of eight anthropomorphic phantoms as well as two example patients. Both sets of data were reconstructed using OS-EM with ten subsets and up to 40 iterations, including compensation for attenuation, scatter, and spatial resolution. Reconstructed images were deconvolved using the van Cittert algorithm and Lucy-Richardson algorithm, both implemented on images represented as standard cuboid voxels or as regional voxels, consisting of regions defined from whole-image segmentation. Methods embedding regional voxels were applied both assuming region-wise uniform activity concentration and incorporating perturbations in the form of cosine series to relax the uniformity assumption. For comparison, images were also processed with the iterative Yang method and MIRD recovery coefficients. Evaluation was performed with respect to the estimated activity concentration for kidneys, spleen, and tumours, as well as the total activity in the images. MAIN RESULTS: Mean activity-concentration errors prior to PVC were (-22.6±11.5) %, (-13.8±2.1) %, and (-7.4±2.8) % for tumours, kidneys, and spleen, respectively. Region-perturbed van Cittert deconvolution with order 4 reduced these errors to (2.3±7.7) %, (0.3±2.2) %, and (4.0±1.6) % while the errors for region-perturbed Lucy-Richardson deconvolution of order 4 were (0.3±8.0) %, (0.0±1.6) %, (2.6±0.5) %. Corresponding results for the iterative Yang method were (2.8±21) %, (-0.3±2.1) %, and (3.8±2.4) % and using MIRD recovery coefficients (-5.0±14.2) %, (-7.1±1.9) %, and (-0.6±3.1) %. SIGNIFICANCE: Region-based PVC improves the accuracy of quantitative SPECT, and the inclusion of cosine perturbations allows for a gradual relaxation of the uniformity assumption.

articles.title: A fast and reliable quality assurance framework for CBCT-based synthetic CTs for adaptive proton radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: Cone beam CT based synthetic CTs (sCTs) enable online adaptive proton therapy by preserving daily patient anatomy without additional acquisition of diagnostic-quality CTs. However, clinical adoption is limited by the lack of fast, reliable quality assurance (QA) methods. This study proposes and evaluates a practical QA workflow to assess sCT suitability for proton dose optimization. Approach:A two-step sCT-QA workflow was developed in which a candidate sCT intended for reoptimization (sCTref) is compared with an independently generated secondary sCT (sCTtest). The workflow combines image based metrics and dose based metrics, with doses derived from recalculating a template proton plan on both sCTs. In this study, the framework was evaluated using a deformably propagated virtual CT (vCT) as sCTref and either a deep learning-based sCT (sCTDL) or an analytically corrected CBCT (CBCTcorr) as sCTtest. Same-day CTs were deformably registered to the CBCT and used as ground truth (CTGT) for evaluation. Thresholds were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation on 182 head and neck (H&N) CT-CBCT pairs. Dose calculation suitability was defined as a gamma pass rate (2%, 1mm) exceeding 95% between dose distributions computed on sCT and CTGT. The method was further tested on an external H&N dataset and on abdominal cases.Main Results:Optimal classification performance was achieved using a combination of image mean absolute error (MAE) and dose MAE. On the H&N test set, the workflow achieved balanced accuracies of 91.2% and 89.7% for the vCT-CBCTcorr and vCT-sCTDL comparisons, respectively, while maintaining a low false positive rate. When applied without modifications to the external H&N and abdominal datasets, balanced accuracy was 94.7% (HN) and 85.0% (abdominal) for vCT-CBCTcorr, and 37.9% (HN) and 61.1% (abdominal) for vCT-sCTDL.Significance:This study introduces a clinically feasible sCT QA workflow for CBCT based adaptive proton therapy and showed promising transferability across datasets.

articles.title: CT-based Node-RADS for standardized evaluation of lymph node metastasis in rectal cancer and its clinicopathological correlates.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lymph node metastasis identification has important clinical implications for treatment decision-making in rectal cancer (RC). To evaluate the diagnostic performance of the CT-based Node Reporting and Data System 1.0 (Node-RADS) for lymph node metastasis risk in treatment-naive RC patients, and to investigate the correlation between the Node-RADS score and clinicopathological factors. METHODS: A single-center retrospective study was performed to RC patients (Aug 2020-Dec 2025) who underwent radical resection surgery and preoperative contrast-enhanced CT examination. Lymph node status was assessed using Node-RADS score ranging from 1 to 5. Sensitivity, specificity, and Youden's index were calculated for different Node-RADS cut-off values. The overall diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves and the area under the curve (AUC). The associations between Node-RADS score and clinicopathological parameters were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 459 RC patients were evaluated, including 174 pN + and 285 pN-. Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 and ≥ 4 have the satisfactory diagnostic performance, with sensitivity/ specificity/Youden's index of 87.36 %/58.25 %/0.46 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 by Reader 1, 89.08 %/54.04 %/0.43 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 by Reader 2, 74.14 %/78.95 %/0.53 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 4 by Reader 1, and 72.99 %/75.44 %/0.48 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 4 by Reader 2, respectively. The AUC of Node-RADS scores were 0.831(95 %CI:0.793-0.864) and 0.806(95 %CI:0.767-0.841) by Reader 1 and Reader 2, respectively. Node-RADS score correlated with pathological T stage, N stage, and lymphovascular invasion. The inter-reader agreement for Node-RADS score were substantial, with weighted kappa values of 0.650. CONCLUSIONS: The CT-based Node-RADS demonstrates stability and satisfactory diagnostic performance for identifying patients with lymph node metastasis in treatment-naive RC.

articles.title: Diagnostic value of 3D pCASL perfusion in glioma grading according to the WHO 2021 classification: a retrospective study of 530 cases.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of three-dimensional pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (3D pCASL) for preoperative grading of gliomas within the 2021 WHO classification framework and to assess protocol-specific tumor blood flow thresholds for differentiating CNS WHO grade 2 from grade 3-4 tumors. METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 530 patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial glial tumors examined between 2011 and 2024. Nineteen non-diffuse CNS WHO grade 1 tumors were retained for descriptive purposes only and excluded from all grading analyses; the primary analytical cohort therefore comprised 511 gliomas (grade 2, n = 75; grade 3, n = 152; grade 4, n = 284). Diagnoses were reassigned within the WHO 2021 framework using the histological and molecular information available for each patient; tumors lacking molecular information required for an integrated WHO diagnosis were designated NOS. All patients underwent 3.0 T MRI with 3D pCASL. Maximum tumor blood flow (maxTBF) and normalized TBF relative to white matter (nTBF WM) and gray matter (nTBF GM) were measured using approximately 30-mm² hotspot ROIs. RESULTS: In gliomas, maxTBF, nTBF WM, and nTBF GM differentiated grade 2 from grade 3-4 tumors, with AUCs of 0.848, 0.833, and 0.84, respectively. The maxTBF threshold was 63.3 mL/100 g/min; AUCs were 0.743-0.768 for grade 2 versus grade 3 and 0.668-0.715 for grade 3 versus grade 4. After exclusion of NOS cases, glioblastomas and grade 4 astrocytomas did not differ significantly in maxTBF or nTBF (pfdr > 0.05). 3D pCASL also differentiated non-enhancing glioblastomas from grade 2 astrocytomas (maxTBF, pfdr = 0.0018; nTBF, pfdr = 0.0036-0.006), with AUCs of 0.78-0.86, a maxTBF cutoff of 64.1 mL/100 g/min, and specificity up to 96%. maxTBF and nTBF moderately correlated with Ki-67 (r = 0.44-0.50; pfdr < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: 3D pCASL provides high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating grade 2 gliomas from high-grade gliomas and grade 2 from grade 3 tumors within the WHO 2021 framework, while remaining fully non-invasive and requiring no contrast agent.

articles.title: S1 radiculopathy presenting as progressive unilateral calf hypertrophy.
articles.abstract: Progressive unilateral calf enlargement is more commonly attributed to vascular, inflammatory, neoplastic, or lymphatic disease than to chronic denervation. We report a 55-year-old female recreational runner with progressive right calf enlargement and long-standing mild low back pain. Lumbar MRI demonstrated multilevel disc herniations, including a right-sided L5-S1 extrusion with compression of the right S1 nerve root. During the initial phase of calf symptoms, calf MRI showed mild asymmetric enlargement of the right posterior compartment with edema-like signal on fluid-sensitive sequences. At later-stage evaluation, 16 months after the initial calf MRI, ultrasound and follow-up calf MRI demonstrated significant interval progression to marked asymmetric enlargement of the right posterior compartment, predominantly involving the medial gastrocnemius and soleus; at a comparable anatomic level, the right soleus cross-sectional area had increased by approximately 58% relative to the prior calf MRI. Ultrasound showed mildly increased echogenicity with preserved fibrillar architecture, without increased color Doppler flow, focal mass, or architectural distortion. MRI confirmed preserved muscle architecture and absence of fatty replacement, consistent with true muscle hypertrophy rather than fatty pseudohypertrophy. Electromyography confirmed chronic right S1 radiculopathy. This case highlights that chronic S1 radiculopathy may present as progressive true calf hypertrophy without fatty replacement and that unilateral calf muscle enlargement with preserved architecture should prompt correlation with lumbar spine MRI and electrodiagnostic findings.

articles.title: Patellar maltracking with dynamic MRI: clinical feasibility and diagnostic utility.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate (1) the clinical feasibility of adding a dynamic MRI sequence during isometric quadriceps contraction to a routine knee MRI protocol and (2) the association between contraction-induced changes and clinically diagnosed patellar maltracking, including whether this information adds discriminative value beyond static imaging. METHODS: This retrospective case-control study included all patellar maltracking patients (cases) and healthy volunteers (controls) undergoing knee MRI supplemented with dynamic series at a single tertiary referral center between 2021 and 2025. Exclusion criteria included prior knee surgery, severe imaging artifacts, or incomplete exams. Image quality, adverse events, and acquisition data were collected. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently performed patellofemoral measurements on the static and dynamic series. Statistical analysis included t-tests, age/sex-adjusted regression, ICC(2,1) for reliability, and AUC/DeLong analysis for incremental diagnostic value. RESULTS: One hundred thirteen patients and 20 controls underwent knee MRI with dynamic series. Image quality was rated "good" or "excellent" in 128/133 (96.2%) subjects. No protocol-related adverse events were recorded. In both cohorts, patellar height, lateral translation, and tilt were greater on dynamic than static series (p < 0.05). There was a larger increase in TT-TG distance between static and dynamic images in patients with patellar maltracking compared to controls (4.35 mm vs 1.58 mm, p = 0.003). Inter-reader ICC(2,1) estimates ranged from 0.36 (95% CI, 0.20-0.50) to 0.93 (95% CI, 0.91-0.95). CONCLUSION: The supplementary dynamic MRI sequence performed during quadriceps contraction is clinically feasible. The contraction-induced increase in TT-TG distance was greater in maltracking patients than controls, though its incremental value beyond static imaging was not statistically confirmed in this sample.

articles.title: Incremental diagnostic value of ultrasound in children with suspected acute appendicitis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In children with suspected acute appendicitis, ultrasound is widely used as first-line imaging, but the incremental diagnostic value of the initial ultrasound report beyond clinical and laboratory variables remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the diagnostic contribution of an appendicitis-compatible initial ultrasound report beyond age, Pediatric Appendicitis Score, and C-reactive protein (CRP), and to describe the role of post-ultrasound computed tomography (CT) within an ultrasound-first pathway. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective single-centre cohort included children aged 3-17 years evaluated for suspected acute appendicitis between May 2025 and March 2026. The primary outcome was histopathologically confirmed appendicitis. Logistic regression compared a clinical model including age, Pediatric Appendicitis Score total, and log2-transformed CRP with an ultrasound-extended model additionally including an appendicitis-compatible initial ultrasound report. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Brier score, likelihood-ratio testing, and DeLong comparison. RESULTS: Among 135 children in the ultrasound-first cohort, 81 had histopathologically confirmed appendicitis and 54 formed the comparison group. The clinical model showed moderate apparent discrimination (AUC 0.771; 95% confidence interval 0.689-0.852; Brier 0.188). In 132 children with classifiable ultrasound reports, addition of an appendicitis-compatible initial ultrasound report increased the AUC from 0.772 to 0.912 and reduced the Brier score from 0.187 to 0.113. Post-ultrasound CT was performed in 52/135 children (38.5%); 29 had appendicitis and 23 did not undergo appendectomy. CONCLUSION: A clear appendicitis-compatible initial ultrasound report provided substantial incremental diagnostic information when added to age, Pediatric Appendicitis Score, and CRP, supporting its role as an integrated component of the diagnostic assessment rather than a standalone test.

articles.title: Thrombosed mycotic aneurysm of the cervical internal carotid artery mimicking a parapharyngeal abscess in a child: a case report of multimodal imaging diagnosis.
articles.abstract: A parapharyngeal abscess, although relatively rare, is a potentially life-threatening deep neck space infection in the pediatric population that carries a risk of serious complications. Mycotic pseudoaneurysm of the cervical internal carotid artery (ICA) is a rare vascular complication in children that can lead to catastrophic hemorrhage if misdiagnosed and attempted for surgical incision. We report a 7-year-old malnourished boy presenting with fever, dysphagia, and neck stiffness. Suboptimal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) suggested a left parapharyngeal abscess, and surgical drainage was planned. A dedicated CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping, magnetic resonance angiography, and three-dimensional CT angiography identified a completely thrombosed mycotic pseudoaneurysm rather than an abscess. This case demonstrates that complete thrombosis transforms a mycotic pseudoaneurysm into a mass that can easily be mistaken for an abscess without the right imaging modalities and high-quality imaging.

articles.title: Cytogenetic biodosimetry for radiotherapy: anthropomorphic phantom-based dose-response calibration and in vivo evaluation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cytogenetic biodosimetry has limited applicability in radiobiological monitoring of radiotherapy due to methodological constraints. To address this problem, we developed and evaluated an inverse biodosimetry approach that included cytogenetic dose-response curve (DRC) construction using an anthropomorphic tissue-equivalent phantom. METHODS: Peripheral blood from a healthy donor was irradiated in vitro with 6 MV linac photons inside a RANDO phantom, reproducing dose distributions of a single radiotherapy fraction for glioblastoma or breast cancer with planned target volume doses 2.0 and 2.67 Gy, respectively. The resulting DRC for dicentric plus centric ring (Dic+CR) yield was fitted to the linear-quadratic model. Its applicability was explored using individual dose-volume data from 12 radiotherapy patients (5 glioblastoma, 7 breast cancer) to calculate expected Dic+CR yields, which were compared with aberration yields observed after the first treatment fraction. RESULTS: The phantom-based DRC showed good agreement with the linear-quadratic model across the investigated dose range. Expected Dic+CR yields calculated from patient-specific dose-volume data were of the same order of magnitude as the observed yields but were lower in 10 of 12 patients. The association between expected and observed yields was positive but not statistically significant (r = 0.39, p = 0.21). CONCLUSIONS: The proof-of-concept for inverse cytogenetic biodosimetry using phantom-based DRC in radiotherapy patients was achieved. Further studies in larger patient cohorts are required to evaluate the influence of in vivo-specific biological factors. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This is the first study integrating an phantom-based cytogenetic DRC with patient-specific dose-volume data for chromosomal biodosimetry in radiotherapy context.

articles.title: Parameter analysis for diffusion tensor imaging corresponding to microstructural alterations following spinal cord injury.
articles.abstract: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is a quantitative MRI technique that enables non-invasive, in vivo evaluation of spinal cord injury (SCI). Based on the anisotropy of water molecule diffusion, DTI provides superior detection of microstructural alterations compared with conventional MRI. Diffusion is quantified by parameters including fractional anisotropy (FA), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), average diffusion coefficient (DCavg), axial diffusion (AD), radial diffusion (RD), and mean diffusion (MD), each showing distinct temporal sensitivity to SCI. Changes in these indices reflect underlying tissue disruption and are closely correlated with neurological function in both experimental and clinical studies. Despite extensive investigations, a systematic summary of their diagnostic and prognostic value has been lacking. This review highlights parameter sensitivity at different injury stages and the associated microstructural changes. AD and DCavg demonstrated high sensitivity in the acute phase, whereas FA was particularly sensitive in the chronic phase. ADC and MD showed mild sensitivity in acute and subacute stages but became more relevant chronically, while RD exhibited low sensitivity in acute phase but progressively increased over time. Collectively, DTI provides critical diagnostic information, and cross-linked analysis of multiple metrics across time points enables more accurate evaluation of SCI severity and prognosis.

articles.title: When extended metabolites profiling helps the prediction of local relapse in glioblastoma: a retrospective study using MRI and MRSI.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study investigates whether integrating postoperative MRI with advanced MR spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) improves voxel-wise prediction of future local recurrence in glioblastoma (GBM). METHODS: Fifty-eight GBM patients included in the clinical trial (XXXXXXXXXXX) were retrospectively analyzed with post-operative baseline for MRI and MRSI processed to generate voxel-level features. MRSI metabolites were quantified using a Bayesian sparse model, enabling reliable estimation of both conventional and extended metabolite panels. Ground-truth relapse labels were derived from longitudinal follow-up MRI to track voxel-wise tissue class changes over time. Voxel-wise relapse prediction was performed using three supervised classifiers (Elastic Net, Random Forest, RBF-SVM) evaluated with leave-one-patient-out cross-validation. Feature sets combining MRI intensities, spatial descriptors, and MRSI metabolites were systematically compared. RESULTS: MRI-only models showed moderate discrimination (AUC ≤ 0.70). Using MRSI features alone significantly improved prediction performance, with further improvements when extending the metabolite basis beyond conventional markers (AUC 0.77 to 0.82, p < 0.001). Spatial descriptors and MRSI-based models provided the largest performance gains (AUC up to 0.95). SHAP analysis consistently identified both conventional and secondary metabolites among the most influential predictors, particularly in the absence of spatial features. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative MRSI and spatial descriptors significantly enhances voxel-wise prediction of GBM relapse, particularly when using an extended metabolite basis beyond conventional markers.

articles.title: Medical Vision Foundation Models: A comprehensive review from technical evolution to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Medical Vision Foundation Models (MVFMs) mark a shift from task-specific artificial intelligence (AI) toward general-purpose visual intelligence in medical imaging. However, clinical deployment remains constrained by tensions among data availability, technological development, and integration into clinical workflows. To address these issues, this review provides a systematic analysis of the field's evolution from 2019 to 2025. We introduce the Data-Technology-Translation Triad as a unifying conceptual framework to structure the progress, key factors, and challenges of MVFMs. Our analysis traces the field's development and identifies a convergence toward Transformer-based and hybrid architectures, alongside hybrid pre-training paradigms. We present a unified technical framework that covers pre-training strategies, including generative, contrastive, and hybrid learning, as well as adaptation mechanisms such as full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompt learning. Furthermore, we examine how data scarcity, heterogeneity, and privacy constraints in medical imaging drive the adoption of self-supervised learning and highlight domain generalization as a critical research direction. Although MVFMs demonstrate strong performance in data-efficient and multi-task settings, their clinical translation is hindered by limited generalization, insufficient interpretability, misalignment with clinical workflows, and regulatory uncertainty. In response, we propose practical directions for developing reliable general-purpose medical vision systems, with emphasis on causal reasoning, dynamic data learning, interactive human-AI collaboration, and coordinated efforts among researchers, clinicians, and regulators. This review provides a structured reference to guide MVFMs from technical validation to clinically effective, reliable, and ethically sound deployment. An updated collection of MVFM papers and related resources is available at our website https://github.com/ice-TuoShui/MVFM-Review.

articles.title: Segment Anything Models for medical image segmentation: From native capabilities to clinical requirements.
articles.abstract: Medical image segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis and precision medicine, yet conventional supervised models depend heavily on high-quality annotations and often generalize poorly across domains. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) family offers a transferable, interactive, and extensible foundation for segmentation, but direct medical transfer remains limited by domain gaps, insufficient modeling of medical semantics and anatomy, and mismatches in high-dimensional volumetric and sequential imaging scenarios. This review critically examines the evolution and native capability boundaries of SAM, SAM 2, and SAM 3. Across generations, native capabilities expand from spatial prompting to sequential propagation and concept-level target specification, without automatically conferring medical expertise. We organize medical adaptation from three connected perspectives: model adaptation and strategy selection, task knowledge organization and utilization, and application-oriented adaptation. Cross-method analysis shows that no strategy is universally optimal; effectiveness depends on the gap between foundation-model capabilities and target-task requirements, together with data scale, domain discrepancy, imaging dimensionality, computational resources, and clinical constraints. We further identify four priorities for clinical translation: standardized evaluation for cross-study comparability, controlled continual adaptation under clinical domain drift, dynamic resource scheduling for high-dimensional and real-time workflows, and uncertainty stratification and clinical reliability control. Overall, further progress depends on accurate capability assessment, condition-matched adaptation, and explicit control of computational and prediction risks.

Noninvasive assessment of renal allograft function with multiparametric MRI: DWI, DTI, and arterial spin labeling compared with eGFR.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and arterial spin labeling (ASL) for noninvasive assessment of renal allograft function using estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as the reference. METHODS: Eighty-four kidney transplant recipients and 30 age-matched healthy volunteers underwent mono-exponential DWI, DTI, and pseudocontinuous ASL on a 1.5-T MRI scanner. Cortical and medullary apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), fractional anisotropy (FA), and cortical renal blood flow (RBF) were measured. Recipients were grouped by eGFR, and intergroup differences, correlations with eGFR, and receiver operating characteristic performance were analyzed. RESULTS: Cortical ADC, medullary ADC, and cortical RBF decreased with worsening allograft function and correlated positively with eGFR (r = 0.513, 0.489, and 0.615, respectively; all p < 0.001). Cortical and medullary FA were not significantly correlated with eGFR. Cortical RBF showed the highest single-parameter area under the curve for differentiating group 1 from group 2 (0.919; sensitivity, 95.7%; specificity, 71.4%) and group 1 from group 3 (0.969; sensitivity, 85.7%; specificity, 100%). When distinguishing group 1 from group 2, the AUCs obtained by combining cortical RBF with cortical ADC or medullary ADC, as well as the combination of all three parameters, were significantly higher than those of cortical ADC alone or medullary ADC alone (P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: DWI-derived ADC and ASL-derived cortical RBF are useful noninvasive MRI markers of renal allograft function, with cortical RBF showing the strongest diagnostic performance. DTI-derived FA appeared exploratory in this cohort.

articles.title: Current practices in elective embolisation: insights from a UK national cross-sectional survey.
articles.abstract: AIM: The aim of this study was to evaluate the national landscape of elective embolisation services in the UK and identify factors affecting service delivery and expansion. MATERIALS AND METHODS: An online cross-sectional survey comprising 19 structured questions exploring the current provision of arterial and venous elective embolisation procedures, service capacity, resource availability, and training was distributed to approximately 1,000 members of a national society in March 2025. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were performed. RESULTS: Eighty-five responses from 54 UK National Health Service (NHS) Trusts were analysed, predominantly from consultant interventional radiologists (85%), working in tertiary centres (62%), district general hospitals (24%), or both (14%). Elective arterial and venous embolisation procedures were widely performed, most commonly uterine artery (94%), renal angiomyolipoma (92%), visceral aneurysm (89%), and varicocele (98%) embolisation. Tumour, type II endoleak, prostate artery, and arteriovenous malformation embolisation were performed significantly more frequently in tertiary centres (P < .05). Most reported access to day-case beds (87%) and clinic time (84%), although provision was frequently perceived as insufficient. While 63% expressed a desire to expand services, key barriers included funding (55%), inadequate referral pathways (45%), bed capacity (39% day-case; 37% inpatient), emergency workload (36%), and workforce shortages (36% radiologists; 36% nurses/radiographers). Qualitative feedback highlighted resource limitations, regional disparities, and the need for more flexible training pathways. CONCLUSION: Sustainable expansion of elective embolisation across the UK requires clinically integrated interventional radiology (IR) services, protected capacity, infrastructure and workforce investment, regional networks, standardisation, flexible training, and systematic evaluation.

articles.title: Defining the Clinical Indication for Real-Time Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ultrasound in Breast Lesions with Low Suspicion of Malignancy.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether real-time artificial intelligence (AI) breast ultrasound (US) can identify a subgroup of breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) category 4A lesions without suspicious mammographic (MMG) findings in whom unnecessary biopsy may be safely avoided. METHODS: This retrospective analysis of single-center biopsy registry included 641 consecutive US BI-RADS 4A lesions that underwent vacuum-assisted breast biopsy. Before conducting biopsy, the lesions were reassessed using a real-time AI US system (CadAI-B®), and MMG findings were classified as suspicious or non-suspicious based on formal reports. Seven prespecified biopsy-decision strategies were evaluated, including 3 AI-only strategies, 3 mammography-gated AI strategies, and the current standard strategy of biopsy all BI-RADS 4A lesions. The primary outcomes were biopsy reduction rate, missed cancers, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy, with final pathology as the reference standard. RESULTS: Among 641 cases of US BI-RADS 4A lesions, 26 cases of malignancies (4.1%) were identified, including 14 cases of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), 11 cases of invasive ductal carcinomas, and 1 case of apocrine carcinoma. AI reassigned 289 cases of lesions (45.1%) to BI-RADS categories 1-3. AI-only biopsy-deferral strategies missed 30.8% and 38.5% of malignancies when biopsy was deferred for AI BI-RADS ≤2 and ≤3 lesions, respectively, with DCIS accounting for most missed cancers. In contrast, among lesions without suspicious MMG findings, no malignancies were observed in AI BI-RADS 1-3 lesions. The sequential strategy of deferring biopsy only for lesions with AI BI-RADS ≤3 and non-suspicious MMG findings reduced biopsies by 43.5% (279/641) while maintaining 100.0% sensitivity (95% CI, 87.1-100.0%) and increasing specificity to 45.4% (95% CI, 41.4-49.4%). CONCLUSION: Real-time AI breast US alone could not safely support biopsy deferral in US BI-RADS 4A lesions. However, after suspicious MMG findings had been excluded, AI identified a low-risk subgroup in whom unnecessary biopsy could be substantially reduced without compromising cancer detection. These findings suggest that the clinical utility of real-time AI breast US lies in patients without suspicious MMG findings. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before clinical implementation.
